alignment.note: The Greek prefixes the clause with καί and additionally carries a postpositive δέ (token 2), giving a doubled connective typical of Markan style; Syriac fuses the conjunction into the verb (ܘܐܫܬܥܝܘ) and Latin renders only Et, both dropping the second connective particle.
διηγήσαντο / ܐܫܬܥܝܘ / narraverunt — 'they recounted', all three in finite plural narrative tense.

The postpositive δέ has no counterpart in either the Syriac or the Latin, which express the connective force solely through the initial conjunction; its omission is a routine stylistic simplification in the versions.
αὐτοῖς / ܠܗܘܢ / illis — dative plural pronoun 'to them'.

Greek uses an articular substantival participle (οἱ ἰδόντες, 'those who saw'); Latin recasts this as a relative clause with a pluperfect (qui viderant); Syriac employs the demonstrative ܗܢܘܢ plus the relative-marked verb ܕܚܙܘ, a double-headed relative construction — semantically equivalent but syntactically distinct.
πῶς / ܕܐܝܟܢܐ / qualiter — interrogative-manner adverb 'how / in what way'.

Greek ἐγένετο is aorist indicative ('it happened'); Latin renders it with the periphrastic pluperfect subjunctive factum esset, as required after qualiter in an indirect question; Syriac ܗܘܐ is a simple perfect, neutral as to mood.

Greek uses an articular present passive participle (τῷ δαιμονιζομένῳ, 'to the one being demon-possessed'); Latin expands into a relative clause with a noun-plus-verb idiom (qui dæmonium habuerat, 'who had had a demon'); Syriac ܠܗܘ ܕܫܐܕܘܗܝ literally 'to him whose demons [were]', a possessive relative phrasing.
Greek and Latin use the plain connective καί / et; Syriac strengthens it to ܘܐܦ ('and also'), an emphatic additive nuance not explicit in the other two witnesses.

Greek marks the noun with the genitive article (τῶν χοίρων); Syriac supplies a demonstrative ܗܢܘܢ before ܚܙܝܪܐ ('those swine'), giving anaphoric definiteness; Latin porcis has no article, definiteness being carried by context alone.
